Verdict: REVISEThe three advertised structural conclusions appear mathematically correct under their intended hypotheses. I found no counterexample to:the straight-strip and straight-link decomposition under  $\deg_P\le 3$ ;the width- $2/3/\ge4$  matching-exit classification under exact occupied degree  $\deg_A=3$ , uniqueness of the matching, and absence of promotion bundles; orthe  $4|J|$  marking and  $1+3b$  surviving-strip bounds.However, the note is not fully self-contained as written. The substantive issue is in Section 3: the supplied promotion lemmas establish the one-color cycle criterion, while the note uses “bundle-terminal” as though it excludes arbitrary bundles with mixed orientations. The missing implication is true, but it needs to be written. There are also several terminology points that should be made explicit, especially the distinction between endpoint degree and occupied degree and the meaning of “contact” versus “matching exit.”With the Section 3 argument added and the terminology tightened, I would accept the note as a structural reduction. As submitted, I recommend REVISE.1. Straight-chamber network theorem1.1 The face-dual argument is correctLet  $H$  be the graph whose vertices are P-faces and whose edges represent shared sides.If one P-face has two neighboring P-faces on perpendicular sides, the two neighboring faces meet at a corner of the original face. The three faces then contain all four grid neighbors of that common corner. Hence that corner has four P-neighbors, contradicting
$$\deg_P(p)\le 3.$$
Therefore every face has at most two face-neighbors, and if it has two, they are on opposite sides. In the square face lattice, this forces every connected finite component of  $H$  to be a straight horizontal or vertical sequence. A direction cannot change without creating perpendicular neighbors, and a finite straight sequence cannot close into a cycle.Thus each face component has the vertex set of a  $2\times w$  rectangle.There is one notation point worth fixing. In the note and Section 3,  $w$  counts vertex columns:
$$\{0,1\}\times\{0,\ldots,w-1\},$$
so a single isolated P-face has  $w=2$ , not  $w=1$ . Equivalently, a strip of  $k$  faces has  $w=k+1$  vertex columns. The current coordinates make the intended convention recoverable, but it should be stated explicitly.1.2 Distinct chambers are vertex-disjointTwo distinct face components cannot share an edge, since edge-sharing would put the faces in the same face component.If they share only a vertex, the two faces occupy opposite quadrants around that vertex. Their four corners then supply all four grid neighbors of the shared vertex as P, giving  $\deg_P=4$ . This is again excluded.Therefore distinct chambers have disjoint vertex sets. This part of the proof is sound.1.3 The residual P-graph is a union of straight pathsLet
$$U=P\setminus \bigcup_C V(C),$$
where the union is over all chambers.The branch lemma gives  $\deg_P(u)\le 2$  for  $u\in U$ : if  $u$  had at least three P-neighbors, it would belong to a P-face and hence would not lie in  $U$ .If  $u\in U$  has two P-neighbors and they are perpendicular, the local turn lemma puts  $u$  in a P-face, again a contradiction. Thus two P-neighbors of a  $U$ -vertex must be collinear.Consequently, each connected component of  $G[P][U]$  is a finite straight path or a singleton. The following details in the note are correct:An internal path vertex has two U-neighbors, so it cannot have an additional chamber P-neighbor; otherwise it would have at least three P-neighbors and the branch lemma would apply.A non-singleton path endpoint already has one path neighbor. It can therefore have at most one chamber P-neighbor.If it has such a chamber neighbor, the path edge and chamber edge must be collinear by the local turn lemma.A singleton can have at most two chamber neighbors. If it has two, they must be opposite rather than perpendicular.For clarity, “contacts” here should be defined as P-edges between  $U$  and a chamber. T-neighbors are irrelevant to this residual P-graph statement.1.4 Chamber contacts occur only at cornersFor a  $2\times w$  chamber:every noncorner vertex has three chamber P-neighbors;every corner has two chamber P-neighbors.Under  $\deg_P\le3$ , a noncorner cannot have an additional P-neighbor. A corner can have at most one external P-neighbor. Hence every  $U$ -chamber edge meets a chamber corner, and each path endpoint contributes at most one such edge.This also covers direct chamber-to-chamber P-edges: if such an edge exists, both endpoints must be corners.A concrete geometric example is possible. Take one P-face with corners  $[0,1]\times[0,1]$  and another with corners  $[2,3]\times[-1,0]$ . The vertices  $(1,0)$  and  $(2,0)$  are adjacent P-vertices, but the two faces are distinct and do not share a face or a corner. The contact edge is a direct chamber-to-chamber edge. The two contact vertices each have three P-neighbors, so this is compatible with  $\deg_P\le3$ . No intervening singleton link is required.Thus the note is right to state explicitly that the chamber quotient need not be a tree and that direct chamber contacts are allowed.1.5 Boundary behaviorThe outside-rectangle extension by blank vertices is adequate for the local turn and branch arguments. A turn at a boundary corner cannot create an exception: if two perpendicular P-faces existed there, all four grid neighbors of the corner would still have to be P, which is impossible when one of those positions lies outside the rectangle.Boundary conditions can make some listed chamber configurations unrealizable, especially matching exits that would have to leave the rectangle. That only removes configurations from the class; it does not invalidate the necessary structural conclusions.Conclusion for Section 2: the theorem is correct. Add the definitions of  $U$ , “contact,” and the vertex-column convention for  $w$ .2. The degree-three matching-exit theoremThe geometric part of Section 3 is correct, but its matching-terminality premise needs a proof repair.2.1 The unique-perfect-matching conclusion needs one missing lemmaThe note says:“The existing cycle criterion implies that  $M$  is the unique perfect matching of  $G[P]$ . … Conversely … a nonempty one-color bundle has a directed cycle … Thus uniqueness is also sufficient for bundle terminality by bipartite promotion completeness.”The problem is that the supplied earlier cycle lemma only directly handles a directed cycle of candidates on one bipartition side. The Bundle Lemma itself allows an arbitrary orientation of each selected matching edge. Therefore, if “bundle-terminal” means that no nonempty feasible promotion bundle of any orientation exists, the note must show why a mixed-orientation feasible bundle also produces a cycle of the relevant kind.The result is true, and the missing argument is short.Let a feasible nonempty bundle select distinct matching edges
$$e_i=x_i y_i,$$
where  $x_i$  is promoted and  $y_i$  is removed. Let  $Y=\{y_i\}$ . Since every P-vertex has occupied degree exactly three, feasibility gives
$$\deg_{A\setminus Y}(x_i)\le 1.$$
One removed neighbor of  $x_i$  is its own mate  $y_i$ . Since  $x_i$  started with three occupied neighbors and must have at most one remaining, at least one additional occupied neighbor must lie in  $Y$ . Hence there is some  $j\ne i$  with
$$x_i\sim y_j.$$
Define a directed graph on the selected matching edges by putting an arc  $i\to j$  whenever  $x_i\sim y_j$ . Every selected edge has outdegree at least one, so this finite digraph contains a directed cycle
$$i_1\to i_2\to\cdots\to i_k\to i_1.$$
The cross-edges
$$x_{i_1}y_{i_2},\ x_{i_2}y_{i_3},\ \ldots,\ x_{i_k}y_{i_1}$$
are pairwise disjoint. Replacing the matching edges  $x_{i_\ell}y_{i_\ell}$  by these cross-edges gives a second perfect matching of  $G[P]$ .In the bipartite grid, the cycle is automatically monochromatic on the  $x$ -side: if  $x_i\sim y_j$  and  $x_j\sim y_j$ , then  $x_i$  and  $x_j$  have the same bipartition color. Thus the cycle also reduces to the one-color cycle criterion used earlier.Conversely, if  $M'\ne M$  is another perfect matching, an  $M$ - $M'$  alternating cycle gives a feasible promotion bundle by promoting the M-endpoints of one grid bipartition color. Each promoted vertex loses its own mate and the second matching neighbor on the alternating cycle, so its residual occupied degree is at most one.Therefore the correct equivalence is:
$$M\text{ is the unique perfect matching of }G[P]
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\text{there is no nonempty feasible promotion bundle},$$
provided “bundle-terminal” is explicitly defined to exclude arbitrary orientations. If “bundle-terminal” is intended to mean only “no one-color bundle,” say so and state the equivalence in that restricted sense.This is the main reason for the overall REVISE verdict.2.2 Exit count and corner restrictionOnce uniqueness is established, the exit classification is sound.For a chamber  $C$ , let  $e(C)$  be the number of matching edges with exactly one endpoint in  $C$ . Since  $C$  has  $2w$  vertices,
$$2|M\cap E(C)|+e(C)=2w,$$
so  $e(C)$  is even.Only corners can support exits. A noncorner already has three P-neighbors inside the chamber. Under  $\deg_A=3$ , it cannot have an external P-neighbor, and an M-exit necessarily goes to an external P-vertex.Thus
$$e(C)\in\{0,2,4\}.$$
The case  $e(C)=0$  is impossible under uniqueness: the chamber would be matched internally, and the full  $2\times w$  rectangle has at least two perfect matchings for  $w\ge2$ . Replacing the internal matching gives a second global perfect matching.2.3 Four exitsIf all four corners exit, the remaining chamber vertices form a  $2\times(w-2)$  rectangle.For  $w\ge4$ , this remainder has at least two perfect matchings, contradicting uniqueness.For  $w=3$ , the remainder is a single vertical edge, so the internal matching is unique.For  $w=2$ , the remainder is empty.Therefore four exits are possible only for  $w=2$  or  $w=3$ , exactly as stated.2.4 Two exits at the same endIf the two exits occupy the two corners of one longitudinal end, the remainder is a  $2\times(w-1)$  rectangle.For  $w\ge3$ , it has at least two perfect matchings, so this pattern is impossible.For  $w=2$ , the remainder is one vertical edge, so the pattern is allowed.2.5 One exit at each endThe remaining two exits must be one at each longitudinal end for all other two-exit cases.Let the left exit be in row  $r\in\{0,1\}$  and the right exit in row  $s\in\{0,1\}$ , with coordinates
$$( r,0),\qquad (s,w-1).$$
The two removed vertices must have opposite bipartition colors, because all remaining internal matching edges connect opposite colors. This gives
$$r+s+w-1\equiv 1\pmod 2,$$
or equivalently
$$s\equiv r+w\pmod2.$$
The internal matching is then forced by successive degree-one propagation from the remaining corner at the left end. The residual graph is a single zigzag path, so there is exactly one matching.The small widths are correctly covered: $w=2$ : the only valid one-at-each-end two-exit patterns are horizontal adjacent pairs. Diagonal exit pairs leave two same-color unmatched vertices and cannot be matched. $w=3$ : two exits must be one at each end and in opposite rows. Four exits are also possible, leaving the central vertical edge. $w\ge4$ : exactly two exits, one at each end, with the stated parity relation.The phrase “same two-end pattern” for  $w=3$  should be made explicit: it means exactly one exit in each longitudinal end column, with the opposite-row parity condition above.2.6 External P-contacts versus matching exitsThe note should emphasize that an exit is an M-edge, not merely an external P-adjacency.A chamber corner may have an external P-neighbor through an ordinary endpoint-graph edge that is not in  $M$ . Such an edge is a geometric chamber contact, but not a matching exit. If the direct chamber-to-chamber edge belongs to  $M$ , it is an exit for both chambers.This distinction matters for later charge arguments, although it does not alter the local exit classification.Boundary blanks may prevent some exit patterns from occurring, but they do not create any additional patterns.3. Localization of geometric turnsSection 4 is correct under the inherited single-terminal hypothesis.Let
$$J=\{p\in P:\deg_P(p)=4\}.$$
A grid vertex lies on at most four unit faces, so marking every P-face containing a member of  $J$  marks at most
$$4|J|$$
faces.After deleting the marked faces, suppose two remaining faces in one residual component had perpendicular face-adjacencies. Their common corner would have all four P-neighbors, so it would belong to  $J$ , and both faces would have been marked. Contradiction.Likewise, if two different residual face components shared a vertex, they could not share an edge, because edge-sharing would put them in the same residual face component. They would therefore meet diagonally at a corner. The two diagonal P-faces force all four P-neighbors of that corner to be P, making the corner a member of  $J$ , which again means the faces should have been marked.Hence all residual face components are straight strips with pairwise disjoint vertex sets.The  $1+3b$  boundTake one initially connected face component in the face-dual graph. The dual graph has maximum degree four.Deleting one face vertex of current degree  $d$  can increase the number of connected components by at most  $d-1\le3$ : its component can split into at most  $d$  pieces. Iterating over  $b$  marked faces gives
$$\#\{\text{surviving strips}\}\le 1+3b.$$
If all remaining faces are deleted, the left-hand side is zero, so the bound still holds.This argument is unaffected by boundary faces, direct chamber contacts, singleton links, or marked faces belonging to different original face components, provided  $b$  is counted within the original component under consideration.The note is also correct that  $J$  is not the same as the occupied-degree-four set. A P-vertex can have
$$\deg_P(p)=3,\qquad \deg_A(p)=4$$
because of one T-neighbor. Such a vertex may matter for matching or promotion arguments even though it is not a geometric four-way P junction. Any later charge argument must retain both notions.4. Required revisionsI recommend the following concrete edits.Define bundle-terminal explicitly. State whether it excludes all feasible bundles or only one-color bundles.Insert the mixed-orientation dependency argument described above, or restrict the claim to one-color bundle terminality.Define contacts. Say that Section 2 contacts are P-edges from residual  $U$ -paths to chamber vertices, while Section 3 exits are M-edges with exactly one endpoint in the chamber.State the inherited single-terminal hypothesis at the beginning of Section 4, since the local turn and branch lemmas depend on it.Clarify  $w$ . State that  $w$  counts vertex columns, so one P-face corresponds to  $w=2$ .Replace “same two-end pattern” for  $w=3$  by “one exit in each longitudinal end column, with opposite exit rows.”Keep endpoint and occupied degree notation separate throughout. In particular, use  $\deg_P\le3$  for the geometric decomposition and  $\deg_A=3$  for the matching-exit theorem.After these repairs, the note remains exactly within its stated scope: it gives a structural decomposition and localization result, but it does not establish a coefficient-one charge ceiling, a global receiver inequality, or donor coverage.
